1.pericope_label: Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour... he saith to every one that he is a fool

schools.summary: Delitzsch decides that the Hebrew means deadly flies rather than dead ones, since the genitive construction matches phrases like instruments of death, and canvasses proposals for dung-flies and for flies bearing contagion from corpses; he also treats the first three verses as one quatrain, notes that the word order throws weight on in the way, and corrects a rendering that would leave the fool without a heart at all. Ellicott prefers to construe the second verse as wisdom leading a man toward his right hand, and records but rejects the Latin reading of the third.

Gill keeps both senses of the flies open, reporting one authority for winter-weakened insects dying in the ointment and another for insects poisonous by nature, and sets aside the anatomical question about the heart in favour of readiness of understanding.

Clarke generalizes the image, that any putrefaction spoils perfume, and works the physical fact that the right hand is stronger and better exercised, taking the pair as figures for self-command and its absence; Wesley notes only that the right hand is the common instrument of action.

Henry explains why a small fault costs an eminent man so much — envy fastens on eminence and makes the worst of the lapses of the celebrated — and concludes that those who profess religion must walk circumspectly, since many eyes watch for their halting.

debates.question: Are the flies dead or deadly?

positions.view: Deadly; the construction is a genitive of quality, and reading it as a plain adjective would be an affected poeticism without parallel.
Either will serve; one authority has winter flies dying in the ointment, another flies poisonous by nature.
The species is beside the point; any putrefaction spoils perfume.

debates.question: What is meant by the wise man's heart being at his right hand?

positions.view: Readiness: his understanding is at hand when he needs it, so that he goes about business with dexterity.
Self-command: the right hand is the stronger and better exercised, and the pair figures the control a wise man keeps over mind and tongue against the fool's want of it.
Direction: better rendered towards his right hand, wisdom leading him that way — the book's recurring concession that wisdom often disappoints yet is undeniably superior to folly.

outliers.note: Turns the proverb into a warning about how quickly a long-built reputation is lost, and concludes that no man can be called safe until he is in paradise.
Supports his reading of the flies from Assyrian word-lists, which show how finely the Semitic languages distinguished varieties of fly.
Records the Latin reading of the third verse, in which the fool's self-conceit attributes folly to everyone else, before rejecting it as less obvious than the sense in which he betrays himself.

themes: Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.
A wise man’s heart is at his right hand; but a fool’s heart at his left.
Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool.

4.pericope_label: If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences... If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads leave not thy place literally of an office, so that the person addressed is a subordinate official, and rejects both Luther's link to the preceding fool and the softer sense of keeping one's composure; on the four hazards he observes that the verbs express possibility rather than certainty, since as predictions they would be false to experience. Ellicott glosses yielding as healing, denies that anyone has traced the connection of these proverbs successfully, and identifies the hedge as a stone wall whose Hebrew phrase inverts a prophet's repairer of the breach.

Gill describes the ruler's wrath as a storm, names two biblical courtiers as instances of folly set on high, notes that horses were scarce in Judea and reserved for princes, and applies the removal of stones to those who shift the landmarks of commonwealths.

Clarke treats submission as the subject's place and duty, reports without endorsing a patristic reading in which the ruler is Satan, calls the misplacement of office a favouritism that has ruined nations, and records a proposal that the biter of the eighth verse is a thorn rather than a serpent; Wesley glosses the yielding as a gentle carriage and the stones as burdens too heavy for the man who lifts them.

Henry reads the whole passage politically, warning subject and prince alike not to force a change: the pit-digger's violence returns on his own head, the hedge is the fence God drew round a ruler's prerogative, the stones are pulled down by a reformer who finds demolition easier than building, and the knotty timber is a people that will not split by force.

debates.question: What does leave not thy place mean?

positions.view: Do not abandon the official post you hold; the man addressed is a subordinate officer.
Humble yourself before him, since submission is your place and duty — advice that extends to any inferior before a superior.
Do not throw up your commission in a passion, despairing of regaining favour.

debates.question: Do the four hazards continue the political argument?

positions.view: No; nobody has traced the connection successfully, the theme is simply caution in large undertakings, and making the undertaking a rebellion forces the sense.
Yes, at every point: pit, hedge, stones and timber are all figures for meddling with a settled government.
The question is left open; what matters is that the verbs state possibilities, not certainties.

debates.question: Whose offences are quieted by yielding?

positions.view: Probably the subject's own — the offences he would commit if he did not restrain himself — rather than the ruler's displeasure.
The ruler's; princes are not implacable, and submission recovers their favour.

outliers.note: States plainly that commentators have failed to trace any connection between the proverbs of this chapter, and declines to supply one.
Reports a patristic allegory in which the ruler is Satan and the counsel is not to despair of mercy, adding that this is true in itself whether or not it is in the text.

themes: If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences.
There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceedeth from the ruler:
Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in low place.
I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth.
He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him.
Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby.
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.

11.pericope_label: Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better... The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the eleventh verse to be about a charmer who comes too late, and reports the Talmudic reading that turns its opening word into a question and a rabbinic fable that makes the master of the tongue a slanderer; he presses the verb of swallowing, charts the fool's speech from absurdity to a madness of presumption and frenzy, and works the grammatical anomalies of the last verse. Ellicott, calling the eleventh verse difficult, follows the Greek in making the master of the tongue a snake charmer, and would introduce the fool's ignorance of the future with and yet.

Gill takes the phrase to mean without a whisper of warning, catalogues the fool's habits of repetition and interruption, turns the wise man's gracious words toward the doctrine of grace, and notes that a fool's labour wearies everyone who has to deal with him.

Clarke reads the serpent that bites before it hisses as the slanderer who insinuates before he speaks plainly, holds that a fool can say as little about the past as the future, and treats the closing clause as a proverb about a man who cannot find his way to the next village; Wesley adds that the charmer's art is mentioned only by way of resemblance.

Henry supplies the practical morals: a babbler grows more violent under contradiction and must be charmed rather than out-talked; seditious talk brings a man to official notice; those who begin foolishly end madly; and the road to the heavenly city is a highway on which wayfaring men, though fools, do not go wrong.

debates.question: Who is the master of the tongue?

positions.view: The snake charmer, whose skill is useless once the bite has happened; so the Greek and most interpreters.
The babbler, whose injury by innuendo answers to a snake that bites before it hisses.

debates.question: What is the force of the fool's ignorance of the future?

positions.view: A concession subordinated to the main clause: he talks on although nobody knows what is coming.
A contrast, better rendered with and yet, between his loquacity and the wise man's cautious silence.
Either a rebuke to his boasting or a mockery of his tautology.
Simply that he can say as little about what is past as about what is coming.

outliers.note: Reports, without adopting, a rabbinic fable in which the beasts ask the serpent what pleasure its bite gives and are told that the slanderer profits no more — a reading that makes the master of the tongue a calumniator, and one the Targum, Jerome and Luther followed.
Digresses from the serpent of this verse to defend his opinion that the creature of the garden narrative belonged to the ape family, remarking that the view has been ridiculed but not disproved.
Reads the gracious words of the wise man as doctrinal rather than social, so that his discourse runs on the grace of the Father, the Son and the Spirit in turn.

themes: Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better.
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself.
The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness: and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.
A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him?
The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city.

16.pericope_label: Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning... Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter

schools.summary: Delitzsch notes that the word for child can mean a servant but never a slave, and on that ground rejects an attempt to date the book by reading the verse as a hit at Herod; he takes the dual of idleness as an intensive rather than a reference to two hands, traces the proverb of sloth to the princes just described, and observes that the Greek rendered the word for thought as conscience. Ellicott records the same range of meaning for child, treats the last three verses as isolated proverbs, and notes that the winged creature is literally a master of wings.

Gill lists young kings under whom nations prospered before defining the fault as childishness of judgment, derives the word for nobles from whiteness and insists that imitation matters more than descent, and identifies the feast-makers as the luxurious princes already described.

Clarke argues that regencies breed civil war or oppression, that a legitimate hereditary right takes long to establish, and that money's power is best shown from Horace; on the last verse he wonders whether carrier pigeons are meant and reproduces an elaborate Targum. Wesley marks the morning as the time for weighty affairs and makes nobility a matter of disposition rather than birth.

Henry supplies the political consequences at every point — the body staggers when the head is giddy, the neglected roof lets in rain until a state's treasure is spent — and gives the chapter its most careful paragraph, on money as what procures everything in this life and nothing for the soul.

debates.question: What is wrong with the child king?

positions.view: Not his age but his judgment; nations have prospered under young princes.
The minority itself; regents disagree and foment civil war or oppress the people, and the prince rules partially once of age.
The word may mean servant, and some read it so, to sharpen the contrast with the nobly born king of the next verse.

debates.question: Do the closing verses belong to the mirror for princes?

positions.view: No; they are isolated proverbs, and the plain English sense of each is the right one.
Yes; the proverb on sloth gains its force from that setting, and the feast-makers are the princes just described.

outliers.note: Leaves the text to prescribe the proper hours for meals and to observe that money's sovereignty was better put by Horace than by any commentator.

Presses the limits of the proverb about money: as an instrument of exchange it answers every occasion of this life, yet of itself it feeds and clothes nobody, and it buys neither pardon nor peace of conscience.

themes: Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!
Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through.
A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry: but money answereth all things.
Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.
